explanations.explanation: "Soon" is the word, friend. The LORD says, "for My salvation is coming soon, and My righteousness will be revealed." (Isaiah 56:1) That's the reason He gives for maintaining justice and doing what is right. I like a promise that doesn't come with a long waiting room.

I get why "later" feels natural. We're used to waiting on big things. But the LORD says His salvation is coming "soon," and His righteousness will be revealed. (Isaiah 56:1) He gives that as the reason to maintain justice and do what is right.

"Slowly" sounds like how my first batch of cookies went in that old kitchen. But the LORD doesn't say that. He says, "My salvation is coming soon, and My righteousness will be revealed." (Isaiah 56:1) The word is "soon."

Yes, the Sabbath. The blessed man "keeps the Sabbath without profaning it and keeps his hand from doing any evil." (Isaiah 56:2) That's a man who holds fast to what is right. The Sabbath shows up again in this passage, so keep an eye out for it.

The Passover is a real feast, friend, and Israel kept it. But it isn't what this verse names. The blessed man "keeps the Sabbath without profaning it and keeps his hand from doing any evil." (Isaiah 56:2) The word to watch is "Sabbath."

Firstfruits were a real offering, so I see why it came to mind. But this verse says something else. The blessed man "keeps the Sabbath without profaning it and keeps his hand from doing any evil." (Isaiah 56:2) Not a firstfruit in sight.

explanations.answer: The LORD will shut me out of His people
explanations.explanation: That's it. The text says, "The LORD will utterly exclude me from His people." (Isaiah 56:3) This is about a foreigner who has already joined himself to the LORD, and the LORD says he shouldn't say it. I'd say that's a man who needed to hear some good news.

explanations.answer: The LORD will take away all of my land
explanations.explanation: Land is a reasonable worry, but it isn't in this verse. The foreigner who has joined himself to the LORD shouldn't say, "The LORD will utterly exclude me from His people." (Isaiah 56:3) The worry is about being shut out of the people, not losing property.

explanations.answer: The LORD will send me back to my country
explanations.explanation: Going home sounds like a believable thing to fear. But the verse says something different. The foreigner shouldn't say, "The LORD will utterly exclude me from His people." (Isaiah 56:3) It's about being shut out from the people of the LORD.

Right. The LORD says the memorial and name He gives is "better than that of sons and daughters." (Isaiah 56:5) He gives it "in My house and within My walls." That's the LORD talking, and I'm not about to add anything to that.
Silver and gold would be a nice comparison, but the LORD doesn't use it. He says the name is "better than that of sons and daughters." (Isaiah 56:5) He gives it in His house and within His walls.
I can see why you went there. Land and cattle were a big deal. But the LORD says the memorial and name are "better than that of sons and daughters." (Isaiah 56:5) That's the comparison He makes.
Not quite, friend. The LORD says, "I will give them an everlasting name that will not be cut off." (Isaiah 56:5) Everlasting is a lot longer than a lifetime. So the name does not stop when they do.
False is right. The LORD says, "I will give them an everlasting name that will not be cut off." (Isaiah 56:5) That is a name with no end. It goes far past a lifetime.

That's the one. The LORD says, "I will bring them to My holy mountain and make them joyful in My house of prayer." (Isaiah 56:7) He is the One doing the bringing. That is a good invitation for a foreigner who was worried about being shut out.
The Jordan is a real river, but it isn't named here. The LORD says, "I will bring them to My holy mountain." (Isaiah 56:7) That's where He says the foreigners are headed.
Goshen is a real place, and it's in the Bible. But the LORD doesn't name it in this passage. He says, "I will bring them to My holy mountain." (Isaiah 56:7) The mountain is the destination.

Joyful it is. The LORD says, "I will bring them to My holy mountain and make them joyful in My house of prayer." (Isaiah 56:7) Picture the foreigner who feared being shut out, now joyful in the house itself. That's a big turnaround.
Prayer and quiet go together in my head too. But the LORD says He'll make them "joyful in My house of prayer." (Isaiah 56:7) The word is joyful, not quiet.
Patient is a good word, and I could use more of it myself. But the LORD says He'll "make them joyful in My house of prayer." (Isaiah 56:7) Joyful is what He promises.

True. The LORD says, "Their burnt offerings and sacrifices will be accepted on My altar." (Isaiah 56:7) That is said about the foreigners who join themselves to Him. Nobody sends them home with a note.
Not this time, friend. The LORD says, "Their burnt offerings and sacrifices will be accepted on My altar." (Isaiah 56:7) That's about the foreigners who join themselves to Him. So the answer is True.

All the nations, yes. The LORD says, "for My house will be called a house of prayer for all the nations." (Isaiah 56:7) That's a wide door. I know a thing or two about being let in, and I never get tired of it.
The sons of Levi are named in other places in the Bible, but not here. The LORD says, "My house will be called a house of prayer for all the nations." (Isaiah 56:7) The word is "all."
I see why you picked that. It's a natural guess. But the LORD says His house "will be called a house of prayer for all the nations." (Isaiah 56:7) That's wider than one nation.
Not quite. The Lord GOD says, "I will gather to them still others besides those already gathered." (Isaiah 56:8) He's not finished. There are still others He will gather.

False, and that's the right call. The Lord GOD, who gathers the dispersed of Israel, says, "I will gather to them still others besides those already gathered." (Isaiah 56:8) He says there are still others. No "that's all, folks" here.
